open_questions: Are the individually inconsistent transit depths explained by spot crossings/detrending errors or by a true depth change? Needs more well-measured transits (3 is minimum).
Why does the SPOC depth (2992 ppm) differ so much from QLP depth (7123 ppm) for the same target? Needs a consistent photometric baseline / difference imaging in another sector.
dossier.public_summary: TESS shows a 14.8-day, about 3-hour dip that repeats three times with a planet-sized depth, flat bottom and no secondary eclipse, but the depth is very different in the two sectors and between the individual transits. With only three detections and lost centroid location we cannot tell if this is a real planet seen through spot/detrending noise or a few blended/artefact dips. An extra sector or ground-based transit that pins down a stable depth is needed to decide.

reasons.why: Depth changes are too large to be statistical scatter and the sector_depths_by_source tool shows the change is not a calibration between products but an apparent change within measurements. A true planet should have a steady diluted depth, so this favours a variable depth from a few blended events / imperfect detrending over a planet, though low SNR makes single-sector bias possible.
reasons.value: sector depths 2992 +/-760 ppm (sector 42, TESS-SPOC) vs 7123 +/-737 ppm (sector 92, QLP), p_constant 0.00009578, depth_change_pct 81.68, sector_depths_by_source verdict changes_within_a_source

reasons.why: Individual transit depths are not consistent at high significance – the whole signal is carried by only three events with mean 4851 ppm. With such a low number of events a single outlier can dominate, increasing the chance a few bad/detrended transits mimic a signal.

Centroid could not place the dip on or off target, so an off-target/blended binary is not ruled out by imaging; the large formal depth error and sectors.p_constant below 0.01 means we cannot separate a planet from a few-good-transit / detrending false positive without more data.
